en: The Parivāra:
The Analysis of the Bhikkhunī Rules,
Second Part
2.10 Section on Offenses Already Committed 1.
Chapter on Defeat (Pārājika):
On account of consenting to physical contact, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of consenting to physical contact, one incurs five offenses.
If a lustful bhikkhunī consents to being grasped by a lustful man below the collarbone and above the knees, it is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
If a bhikkhu touches body with body, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
If one touches what is connected to the body with the body, it is an offense of thullaccaya;
if one touches what is connected to the body with something connected to the body, it is an offense of dukkaṭa;
for tickling with the fingers, it is an offense of pācittiya.
On account of consenting to physical contact, one incurs these five offenses.
On account of concealing a fault, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of concealing a fault, one incurs four offenses.
If a bhikkhunī knowingly conceals an offense involving defeat (pārājika), she incurs an offense of defeat;
if she conceals it while being in doubt, she incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya);
if she conceals a saṅghādisesa offense committed by a bhikkhu, she incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If he conceals a failure in conduct, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
On account of concealing a fault, he incurs these four offenses.
How many offenses does he incur on account of not relinquishing [his position] despite being pressed up to three times?
On account of not relinquishing [her position] after being exhorted up to three times, she incurs five offenses.
When a nun who follows one who has been suspended does not relinquish [her position] after being exhorted up to three times: there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) with the motion (*ñatti*);
with two proclamations (*kammavācā*), there are offenses of grave wrongdoing (*thullaccaya*).
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*);
if a nun who sides with a schismatic does not desist after being admonished up to three times, there is an offense of formal meeting (*saṅghādisesa*);
if she does not relinquish a wicked view after being admonished up to three times, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Due to not relinquishing [the course of action] after being exhorted up to the third time, one incurs these five offenses.
Due to the fulfillment of the eighth basis, how many offenses does one incur?
Due to the fulfillment of the eighth basis, one incurs three offenses.
If she goes because she has been told by a man, “Come to such-and-such a place,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
as soon as she enters the reach of the man’s hand, there is an offense of grave transgression (thullaccaya);
when she completes the eighth constituent, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
By fulfilling the eighth basis, one incurs these three offenses.
The section on the *pārājika* offenses is concluded.
2. The Section on the *saṅghādisesa* Offenses, etc.
A quarrelsome nun incurs three offenses by reason of initiating a lawsuit:
when she informs one person, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
when she informs a second person, there is an offense of grave misconduct (thullaccaya).
At the conclusion of the motion, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
On account of giving full admission to a female thief, one incurs three offenses:
for the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); ... [and so on].
With two proclamations, there are thullaccaya offenses;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
On account of traveling to another village, one commits three offenses.
As he goes, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
when he steps over the first boundary, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya);
when he steps over the second foot, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).

If one reinstates a nun who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction—without having obtained the permission of the performing Saṅgha and without knowing the consent of the group—one incurs three offenses on account of the reinstatement:
an offense of wrong-doing for the motion;
two offenses of serious transgression for the two subsequent proclamations.
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
A lustful nun, having personally accepted from the hand of a lustful man either fresh food or cooked food, incurs three offenses by reason of eating it:
if she accepts it with the thought, "I will eat it, I will consume it," there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
With every swallow, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
If she accepts water for rinsing the mouth or a tooth-stick, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
[If he says: "What can this man do to you, Noble Lady, whether he is lustful or not, since you yourself are free from lust?"...
“Come now, noble lady, please accept with your own hand whatever hard food or soft food this person gives you, and eat or consume it.
On account of such instigation, one incurs three offenses.
If, at his word, she accepts it thinking, “I will eat it, I will consume it,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful, there is an offense of thullaccaya;
at the conclusion of the meal, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
Due to a nun’s failure to desist after being admonished up to three times when she is angry, one incurs three offenses.
With the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
with two proclamations, there are offenses of serious transgression;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension from the Saṅgha.
When a nun has been rebuked in some legal matter and does not desist after being formally admonished up to three times, she incurs three offenses on account of that non-desistance:
a *dukkaṭa* for the motion (*ñatti*);
two *thullaccaya*s for the two formal proclamations (*kammavācā*).
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
A nun who is in association [with a layman] incurs three offenses by reason of not relinquishing [her behavior] after being exhorted up to the third time:
for the motion (*ñatti*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);...
With two formal proclamations (*kammavācā*), there are offenses of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*);
at the conclusion of the formal proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).

By urging [the nuns], saying, "Venerable ladies, you should indeed live in association; do not live apart," she incurs three offenses on account of not relinquishing [her position] after being admonished up to the third time.
There is an offense of wrong-doing for the motion;
there are offenses of serious transgression for the two formal proclamations;
at the conclusion of the formal proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension from the Saṅgha.
The ten *saṅghādisesa* rules are concluded … [as above, they should be expanded in detail; the only difference is the condition].
How many offenses does one commit by asking for curd and then eating it?
Having requested curd, one incurs two offenses by reason of eating it:
when one accepts it with the intention, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
Having requested curd, one incurs these two offenses as a result of eating it.
The second section on the occurrence of offenses is finished.
